source_title: Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War, Massacre of Cheyenne Indians (1865), testimony of S. G. Colley
source_cite: JCCW 1865, Massacre of Cheyenne Indians, p. 32 (Colley); p. 57 (newspaper exhibit)
source_quote: Black Kettle was not killed, but Left Hand was wounded, and died after he got over there.
corrected_summary: Sand Creek killed a number of Cheyenne chiefs and headmen (White Antelope and One Eye among them; Coel counts nine Council of 44 members), and the Arapaho leader Left Hand was reported wounded and later died. Little Robe should not be listed among the dead: a Little Robe signed the Oct. 1865 treaty, the Nov. 1866 assent and the 1867 Medicine Lodge treaty, and was named in 1865 Art. 6 as a surviving Sand Creek chief. Early 1864 reports that listed Little Robe and Black Kettle as killed were wrong. The claim that this destroyed leadership needed for treaty-making is the source's (and Coel's) argument.
notes: Nine-member count is Coel 1981 (scholarly, not checked). Lean Bear 1864 killing not checked here. The JCCW report (p. 57) reprints a newspaper list ("Among the killed were all the Cheyenne chiefs, Black Kettle, White Antelope, Little Robe, Left Hand, Knock Knee, One Eye") that is demonstrably wrong about Black Kettle and Little Robe; that list is the likely origin of the Little Robe error. Little Robe as 1865 signer and Art. 6 grantee: 14 Stat. 706-707.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861; Treaty of the Little Arkansas, Oct. 14, 1865
source_quote: all the lands now owned, possessed, or claimed by them, wherever situated, except a tract to be reserved for the use of said tribes
corrected_summary: Land north of the South Platte was unceded when gold-rush settlement began in 1858-60. On paper it was then ceded: the 1861 Fort Wise treaty ceded all lands claimed except a reserve, and the 1865 Little Arkansas treaty again relinquished the country between the Platte forks, the Rockies and the Arkansas. The tribes contest the validity of those cessions. Map as "ceded on paper, contested", not "never ceded".
notes: Homestead/Preemption point and the Colorado Encyclopedia quote not checked against primary text; it is a legal argument by the source. Peace Commission 1868 (p. 6) independently says the gold-seekers "possessed nothing more than the right of transit" and took the land "against the protests of the Indians".

source_title: Pacific Railway Act, July 1, 1862, ch. 120, sec. 2
source_quote: extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles to all lands falling
notes: Statute quote confirmed (OCR "ibr" = "for"). The Usher remark about clearing the Platte and Republican valleys rests on Berthrong 1963, 231 and was not checked.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024, Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho chapter
source_quote: to pay no attention to any peace movements or propositions
notes: Would be settled by the Stanton, Dodge and Ford correspondence in War of the Rebellion: Official Records, ser. I, vol. 48, pts. 1-2, and H. Exec. Doc., 39th Cong., 1st sess. (the source's endnote 7). Not in the local library. The Dodge "kill every male over 12" order has no endnote in the source; treat as unverified.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024, quoting Powell 1981
source_quote: having been forced, in self-protection, to fight the United States troops under the command of Colo
notes: The August 1865 truce text (Leavenworth/Sanborn, mouth of the Little Arkansas, Aug. 15, 1865) is printed in ARCIA 1865, not in the local library. Searched ARCIA 1866, Doolittle 1867 and JCCW 1865: no match. ARCIA 1865 would settle it.

source_title: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 14, 1865 (Little Arkansas)
source_cite: 14 Stat. 703, preamble, Art. VIII, signature block 707
source_quote: of the respective tribes not now present to unite with them and accede
corrected_summary: The treaty text recites that the signers were "duly authorized", but its own Art. 8 admits that parts of both tribes were "not now present". Six Cheyennes signed (four chiefs: Black Kettle, Seven Bulls, Little Robe, Black White Man; two headmen) and eight Arapahos. The Commissioner of Indian Affairs reported in 1866 that the Dog Soldiers "did not unite with their people in the treaty". That the commissioners told signers they signed only for their own bands, and the 8-of-280 lodge count, are Powell's accounts (not checked).
notes: ARCIA 1866 p. 9 (Commissioner Cooley) confirms the Dog Soldier absence. Royce 477 = the 1861 Fort Wise reserve ceded by this treaty; 426 = 1865 cession of claim. Local Kappler OCR is the 1903 printing with different page numbers.

source_title: Treaty with the Apache, Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 17, 1865
source_quote: they are hereby united, and the United States will hereafter recognize said tribes as the confederated bands or tribes of Cheyenne, Arrapahoe, and Apache Indians.
corrected_summary: The "confederated tribes" provision was not an amendment added to the Oct. 14 treaty. It is a separate treaty dated Oct. 17, 1865, between the U.S. and the Apache, Cheyenne and Arapaho, which brought the Apache into the Oct. 14 treaty. The Oct. 14 treaty itself already called the Cheyenne and Arapaho "confederated tribes". Whether Cheyenne and Arapaho leaders understood or agreed to the Oct. 17 instrument is Berthrong's claim and was not checked against its signature list.
notes: The Apache assent to the Senate amendments (Nov. 19, 1866) at 14 Stat. 709-710 recites this Oct. 17 treaty. Signature list of the Oct. 17 treaty not legible in the local Kappler OCR.

source_title: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 14, 1865 (Little Arkansas)
source_cite: 14 Stat. 703, 705-706, Arts. V and VI; Senate amendment 2, p. 708
source_quote: grant three hundred any twenty acres of land by patent to each of the following-named chiefs of said bands
corrected_summary: The treaty (Art. 6) granted 320 acres each to four named surviving chiefs (Black Kettle, Seven Bulls, Little Robe, Black White Man), 160 acres to each person widowed or orphaned at Sand Creek, and money or goods for property destroyed, per a schedule. Art. 5 granted 640 acres each to named relatives of mixed descent, to be selected from the 1861 Fort Wise reserve. That these were never delivered is the source's statement; no primary record of nonpayment was checked.
notes: Prior status "confirmed" downgraded: the nonpayment claim is book-only. The reader note (320 acres to survivors who lost a husband) is wrong: 320 acres went to the four named chiefs. Art. 5 lands were to come from the Fort Wise reserve, which this same treaty ceded (Royce 477). The Senate added a proviso to Art. 5 barring locations on lands already granted to others. Nonpayment would be settled by ARCIA 1866-1870 and Interior land records.

source_title: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 14, 1865 (Little Arkansas)
source_cite: 14 Stat. 705, Art. VI; Senate amendment 3, 14 Stat. 708
source_quote: 3d. Art ic le VI. page 8, lines 4 and 5, strike out the words
corrected_summary: The treaty (Art. 6) condemns and repudiates "the gross and wanton outrages" at Sand Creek against Indians who were at peace under the U.S. flag. But the Senate struck the words naming Colonel J. M. Chivington and U.S. troops before ratifying. The treaty was superseded by Medicine Lodge in 1867, and its reservation was never established.
notes: Quote is from the Senate amendment; the stricken words are "by Colonel J. M. Chivington, in command of United States troops." This is a consequential detail for any "the U.S. acknowledged Sand Creek" label.

source_title: Report of the Indian Peace Commissioners, Jan. 7, 1868 (H. Exec. Doc. 97, 40th Cong., 2d sess.)
source_cite: Peace Commission Report 1868, p. 10; 14 Stat. 704-705, Arts. II-III
source_quote: this provision deprived them of any home at all, except the hunting privilege reserved by the treaty.
notes: Art. 2 proviso (no settlement until other Indian claims extinguished) and Art. 3 (range between the Arkansas and Platte until removal) confirmed in 14 Stat. 704-705. The federal Peace Commission itself called the treaty "rendered nugatory by the Senate".

source_title: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1866
source_cite: ARCIA 1866, p. 9 (Commissioner) and Central Superintendency, report of the escort officer, Feb.-Mar. 1866
source_quote: The Indians appear to have construed their signature to the paper forwarded by Major Wynkoop as only a general consent of friendship with the whites, but not as surrendering the Smoky Hill country.
corrected_summary: In Feb.-Mar. 1866 Wynkoop distributed goods and then had Medicine Arrows, Big Head and other Dog Soldier leaders sign a paper binding them to the 1865 treaty; the escort officer told them he would "enforce the treaty to the letter", and Big Head objected to the Smoky Hill route. The Commissioner himself reported that the signers understood it as a pledge of friendship, not a surrender of the Smoky Hill country. "Bribing" and "threatening" are Berthrong's characterizations. The Leavenworth complaint was not checked.
notes: Strong federal admission that the Smoky Hill cession was not understood or agreed to by the Dog Soldiers. Map the Smoky Hill portion of Royce 426 as contested.

source_title: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 14, 1865 (Little Arkansas), Senate amendment and assent
source_cite: 14 Stat. 708-709 (Senate resolution May 22, 1866; assent at Fort Zarah Nov. 10, 1866)
source_quote: shall designate for said tribes a reservation, no part of which shall be within the State of Kansas
notes: Senate authorship of the Kansas proviso is now confirmed (amendment 1, May 22, 1866), resolving the earlier "not seen" note. Assent signers Nov. 10, 1866 include Black Kettle, Little Robe and Big Head (Cheyenne) and Little Raven (Arapaho). Peace Commission 1868 p. 10 says the amendment left them without any home. Dog Soldier non-recognition is consistent with ARCIA 1866. Black Kettle's repudiation of the Smoky Hill cession not checked.

source_title: Report of the Indian Peace Commissioners, 1868
source_quote: he at once ordered the Indian village, of about three hundred lodges together with the entire property of the tribes, to be burned.
corrected_summary: Hancock marched cavalry, infantry and artillery toward a Cheyenne-Sioux village on Pawnee Fork in April 1867; the people fled, fearing another Sand Creek, and Hancock ordered the village of about 300 lodges burned after news that fleeing Indians had attacked a Smoky Hill station. The Peace Commission said this made "the Indian ... an outlaw" on the plains. The 1,400-troop figure, the April 19 date and the Sherman "coaxed out ... or killed" quote are from Berthrong and were not checked.
notes: Federal account context: the burning followed a station attack. The Commission called the war started this way a needless one.

source_title: Act of July 20, 1867, ch. 32 (Indian Peace Commission act)
source_quote: not exceeding four thousand men in number, and for such term of service as, in his judgment, may be necessary for the suppression of Indian hostilities.
corrected_summary: The act said that if the commissioners failed to secure the Indians' consent to remove to reservations and failed to secure peace, the Secretary of War could accept up to 4,000 mounted volunteers "for the suppression of Indian hostilities". The act authorized this; it did not order it, and it does not use the words "force onto reservations".
notes: The threat structure (consent or volunteers) is real and in the statute.

source_title: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 28, 1867 (Medicine Lodge); Commissioner Parker to Secretary Cox, Aug. 10, 1869
source_quote: TALL BULL
corrected_summary: Fourteen Cheyennes (including Bull Bear, Tall Bull and White Horse of the Dog Soldiers, and Black Kettle) and eight Arapahos signed. Roman Nose did not sign. In 1869 the Commissioner of Indian Affairs reported that the tribes "did not understand the location of the reservation" and had never been on it. That gifts and destitution motivated signing is the Colorado Encyclopedia's inference.
notes: Short quote is the signature line "O-TO-AH-HAS-TIS, Tall Bull" (15 Stat. 598). Parker quote at Kappler I 841: "the Cheyennes and Arapahoes did not understand the location of the reservation". The Medicine Lodge reservation (Cherokee Outlet portion) has no Royce number in the atlas crosswalk; it was ceded by 26 Stat. 1022 Art. I.

source_title: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 28, 1867 (Medicine Lodge)
source_cite: 15 Stat. 596, Arts. X-XI; 15 Stat. 594, Art. II
source_quote: on any lands south of the Arkansas so long as the buffalo may range
notes: Art. 2 boundaries: Kansas line (37th parallel) from the Arkansas west to the Cimarron, down the Cimarron to the Arkansas, up the Arkansas. Art. 11 three-year bar on white settlement of the 1865 reserve and Art. 10 thirty years of clothing and $20,000 confirmed. That no reservation was established is confirmed by Parker 1869 ("they have never been upon said reserve", Kappler I 841) and ARCIA 1872 p. 42 ("persisted in a refusal to locate").

source_title: National Park Service, "What Happened to the Bison?"
source_quote: the Army provided free ammunition to hide hunters, who brought bison to the brink of extinction
notes: NPS does say this, but NPS is secondary. Would be settled by the Report of the Secretary of the Interior for 1873 (Delano), not in the local library (ARCIA 1873 does not contain it). Delano's often-quoted 1873 language differs from the NPS paraphrase; do not present the NPS wording as a direct quote. Army ammunition claim needs Army records. 7.5 million figure (Berthrong 1963, 381) not checked.

source_title: George W. Manypenny, Our Indian Wards (1880)
source_quote: He had decided on a winter campaign, the objects of which were
corrected_summary: Manypenny (former Commissioner of Indian Affairs) wrote that of the $500,000 Congress gave Sherman to carry out the 1867-68 treaties, only $50,000 went to Hazen's southern district, that Sherman sought to stop all goods to the Cheyennes and Arapahos, and that Sheridan stockpiled over a million rations for his winter campaign while feeding the tribes was "the simple performance of an obligation, under the treaties of Medicine Lodge creek". In the pages read he does not say treaty money was diverted to the campaign.
notes: Manypenny is a contemporary polemic, not an audit. A diversion claim would need War and Interior accounts for the $500,000 appropriation (Act of July 27, 1868).

source_title: PSL TREC 2024, quoting Berthrong 1963, 344
source_quote: The Battle of Summit Springs thus ended Cheyenne occupation and use of the region between the Platte and Arkansas rivers.
notes: Commonly dated July 11, 1869. The 52-killed figure and Tall Bull's death would be settled by Maj. E. A. Carr's report in the Annual Report of the Secretary of War 1869 (Sheridan's report), not in the local library. Tall Bull signed Medicine Lodge (15 Stat. 598). Category MASSACRE is the reader's; the source calls it a battle.

source_title: Executive order of Aug. 10, 1869 (Parker recommendation approved by Cox and Grant)
source_quote: did not understand the location of the reservation as defined by the treaty of August 19, 1868; that they have never been upon said reserve, and do not desire to go there
corrected_summary: On Aug. 10, 1869 Grant approved the Commissioner's recommendation to locate the Cheyennes and Arapahos on the North Fork of the Canadian. The federal record says this was at the tribes' own request after they had refused the Medicine Lodge reservation. The Commissioner called the land "public land" and said Congress should later confirm a permanent reservation, which it did not do before 1891. ARCIA 1872 put the area at 4,011,500 acres. That this shows treaties were "arbitrary" is the source's argument.
corrected_instrument_cite: Executive order of Aug. 10, 1869, Kappler I (1904) 841
notes: Royce 525 entry: "President establishes a reservation for them on N. fork of Canadian river, in lieu of one designated by treaty of Oct. 28, 1867."

source_title: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, sec. 13, Art. IV; Royce Schedule area 540a
source_quote: in that part thereof now occupied and claimed by the Wichita and affiliated bands of Indians
corrected_summary: The Wichita and affiliated bands were assigned part of the Cheyenne-Arapaho executive-order reservation (between the Washita and the Canadian, from the 98th meridian to 98 degrees 40 minutes) under an Oct. 19, 1872 agreement that Congress never ratified. The 1891 act still excluded that area from Cheyenne-Arapaho allotment. The 760,000-acre figure was not checked.
notes: Royce 540a: reserve "set apart for the Wichita and affiliated bands ... by the unratified Oct. 19, 1872 agreement". Taking by unratified agreement is a stronger point than the source makes.

source_title: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1872
source_quote: a contract, made subject to the action of Congress, was entered into between the Commissioner of Indian Affairs and the delegation of the Arapaho tribe
corrected_summary: In 1872 an Arapaho delegation in Washington signed a contract, subject to Congress, giving up their interest in the Medicine Lodge reservation for a separate reserve; the Commissioner planned "separate negotiations" with the Cheyennes later, so no Cheyennes took part. It was never ratified: the Medicine Lodge reservation was still being ceded in 1891 (26 Stat. 1022, Art. I). The Commissioner claimed the delegation was "fully empowered"; "under pressure" is the source's characterization.
corrected_instrument_cite: Unratified Arapaho agreement of 1872 (ARCIA 1872 p. 42); Act of May 29, 1872 authorizing negotiation
notes: Resolves the note: the 1872 agreement was unratified, consistent with the source's later statement that the Outlet land was ceded only in 1890-91.

source_title: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1883, Cheyenne and Arapaho Agency (Agent Miles)
source_quote: At an annual rental of 2 cents per acre, amounting to
corrected_summary: Agent Miles reported 1883 grazing leases to seven lessees covering 3,117,880 acres at 2 cents per acre ($62,350.60 a year), not about 2.4 million. The bribery of tribal members and staff, the 426,202-acre restriction, Miles's monopolies and Cleveland's 1885 expulsion rest on Berthrong 1976 and were not checked.
notes: Miles's own report praises the leases. Cleveland's removal proclamation (July 23, 1885) would settle the expulsion; Berthrong 1976 the bribery.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024, citing Hagan 2003
source_quote: It was often difficult to determine whose side the attorneys were on.
notes: Hagan 2003 (Taking Indian Lands) is not openly available (archive.org lending only). The 10 percent contract and $67,000 payment would be settled by Hagan or Sen. Exec. Doc. on the Jerome Commission. The source's "May 1869" is a typo for 1889.

source_title: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, ch. 543, sec. 13 (Cheyenne-Arapaho agreement of Oct. 1890)
source_quote: is hereby accepted, rati- fied and confirmed
notes: Ratifying cite confirmed. The Jerome threats ("the law of Congress will be put in force", "will starve") and the halved beef ration need the Cherokee Commission council journal (printed in Sen. Exec. Doc. 1891) or Hagan 2003, 64-65, 79; not reached.

source_title: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, ch. 543, sec. 13 (Cheyenne-Arapaho agreement of Oct. 1890); Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 28, 1867 (Medicine Lodge) Art. XII
source_quote: by Left Hand, his mark, and five hundred and sixty- four others, on the part of the said Indians
corrected_summary: Medicine Lodge Art. 12 required three-fourths of adult males to sign any cession of the reservation. The ratified 1891 text records 565 signatures (Left Hand and 564 others). Noble's instruction, Agent Ashley's 618 adult-male count and Berthrong's estimate that about 680 were needed are from Hagan and Berthrong (not checked). The January 1891 protest by seven Cheyenne chiefs was not checked.
notes: Art. 12 number confirmed (15 Stat. 597). 565 signatures is more than the 464 Ashley said were needed; whether 565 reached three-fourths depends on the disputed adult-male count.

source_title: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, ch. 543, sec. 13 (Cheyenne-Arapaho agreement of Oct. 1890)
source_quote: and all other lands or tracts of country in the Indian Territory to which they have or may set up or allege any right, title, interest or claim whatsoever.
corrected_summary: The 1891 agreement ceded the Medicine Lodge reservation tract in the Cherokee Outlet "absolutely" (Art. 1) and the executive-order reservation subject to allotment (Art. 2), plus any other lands they might claim. The words "any rights they might have" are Hagan's paraphrase of Jerome, not the ratified text. Noble's "pay twice" instruction was not checked.
notes: Art. 1 tract (Arkansas River, Kansas line, Cimarron) is the Medicine Lodge reserve. The Cherokee claim to the same Outlet land supports the overlap point.

source_title: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, ch. 543, sec. 13 (Cheyenne-Arapaho agreement of Oct. 1890)
source_cite: 26 Stat. 1024, Arts. V and VII; 26 Stat. 1025, sec. 15
source_quote: should any In- dian entitled to allotments hereunder fail or refuse to make his or her selection of land in that time, then the allotting, agent in charge of the work of making such allotments shall
corrected_summary: Confirmed: allotting agents assigned allotments to Indians who did not choose within 90 days (Art. 5), and the total price was $1,500,000 (Art. 7). The ratified text gives no per-acre price; "50 cents per acre" and the retained/school/military/opened acreages (Berthrong 1976, 175) were not checked. The same act paid the Choctaw and Chickasaw $2,991,450 for their claimed interest in 2,393,160 acres of the same reservation south of the Canadian (sec. 15).
notes: The Choctaw-Chickasaw payment is useful context: the U.S. paid another nation about twice as much for a residual claim to part of the land as it paid the occupying tribes for the whole. April 19, 1892 opening not checked (ARCIA 1892 search inconclusive).

source_title: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861; ICC compromise settlements
source_quote: all the lands now owned, possessed, or claimed by them, wherever situated, except a tract to be reserved for the use of said tribes
corrected_summary: Boulder was settled in 1858-59 (not 1851) on land then unceded, inside the 1851 Fort Laramie area. On paper the 1861 Fort Wise treaty then ceded it, and the ICC later paid compromise awards for the 1851 area ($15,000,000 to the Southern tribes in 1965; $4,360,886.19 to the Northern Cheyenne in 1963). "Stolen property, never compensated" is the TREC's position; it is accurate only in the sense that no payment was specific to the site and the tribes reject the 1861 cession.
notes: Attribute "unceded" and "stolen" to the tribe/TREC. Do not map as fact.

source_title: Indian Claims Commission, Final Report (1978/79), case index
source_cite: 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162 (findings), 185 (opinion), Oct. 18, 1965, Dkts. 329-A and 329-B
source_quote: Cheyenne and Arapaho 16 162 Findings - Compromise settlement 10/18/65 $15,000,000.. 00
notes: Amount, date and dockets confirmed from the ICC's own case index. The Watonga vote (338 to 2), notice to 1,542 members, and the $1,500,000/4,608,878-acre figure were not checked (would need 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162 itself). The inflation comparison is the source's.

source_title: Indian Claims Commission Act, Aug. 13, 1946, secs. 20(b) and 22
source_quote: either party may appeal from the determination of the Commission to the Court of Claims
corrected_summary: The ICC Act let "either party" appeal a final determination to the Court of Claims, and made payment a "full discharge" of all claims in the controversy. A compromise settlement ends appeal rights for both sides by consent. The TREC's claim that the tribes were barred from appealing while the government could appeal is contradicted as a description of the statute; whether a specific request to reserve appeal rights was refused in this settlement was not checked. The settlement cite is 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162, not 612.
notes: The "valuations biased" and "1851 issues unresolved" points are tribal positions. 17 Ind. Cl. Comm. 612 is the Spokane decision; 612 is a cite error.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Wise, Senate amendment and assent
source_quote: In consideration of the kind treatment of the Arapahoes and Cheyennes by the citizens of Denver City and the adjacent towns, they respectfully request that the proprietors of said city and adjacent towns be permitted
notes: Article 11 is now identified: it asked that Denver and nearby town proprietors be allowed to buy the town lands at $1.25 an acre; the Senate struck it Aug. 6, 1861. 12 Stat. 1168 prints an assent "in full council" with the date in square brackets, [Oct. 29, 1861], signed by the same ten chiefs. The brackets show an editor supplied the date, which is consistent with, but does not prove, the tribe's concern. The erasure and signature allegations can be settled only by the original in NARA RG 11, Ratified Indian Treaty no. 315.

source_title: Report of the Indian Peace Commissioners, 1868; Fort Laramie treaty 1851 Art. 5
source_cite: Peace Commission Report 1868, p. 6; Kappler II (1904) 594
source_quote: thousands of fortune-seekers, who possessed nothing more than the right of transit over these lands, took possession of them for the purpose of mining, and, against the protests of the Indians, founded cities
corrected_summary: The 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho territory ran to the main range of the Rockies, and the federal Peace Commission (1868) agreed the 1858-61 miners had only a right of transit and took the land over Indian protests. "Legally titled" and "never compensated" are tribal positions: the 1861 and 1865 treaties ceded the area on paper and the ICC paid compromise awards for it. The 100,000-trespasser, 4-million-acre school land and 19,000-acre CSU figures were not checked.
notes: Attribute to the tribe/TREC. The Peace Commission quote is a strong federal admission for the 1858-61 period only.

source_title: Act of Feb. 28, 1877, ch. 72, ratifying the agreement of Sept. 26, 1876
source_quote: the Government shall erect for each of the principal chiefs a good and comfortable dwelling-house" said article not having been agreed to by the Sicux Nation
corrected_summary: Art. 6 of the 1876 agreement did promise a house for each principal chief if the Indians moved to Indian Territory. Congress did not ratify that clause (or Art. 4 on removal) because the Sioux had not agreed to it. "Unlawful use of bribery" is the author's characterization (endnote 58).
corrected_instrument_cite: Agreement of Sept. 26, 1876, ratified by Act of Feb. 28, 1877, ch. 72, 19 Stat. 254
notes: Royce 597 (1868 unceded territory), 598 (Black Hills), 599 (northern addition).

source_title: Act of Feb. 28, 1877, ch. 72, ratifying the agreement of Sept. 26, 1876
source_quote: the same was executed by the above Ogallalla Sioux, Chey- ennes, and Arapahoes, at Red Cloud agency, on the 20th day of Sep- tember, A. D. 1876
corrected_summary: The five Cheyenne marks (Living Bear, Spotted Elk, Black Bear, Turkey Legs, Calfskin Shirt) appear with the Oglala and Arapaho signers at Red Cloud Agency in September 1876, per the official interpreter's certificate. The line "Dated and signed at Spotted Tail agency, Nebraska, September 23, 1876" heads the Brule list. There is no Sept. 28, 1877 date, and Congress ratified the agreement on Feb. 28, 1877. The author's broader point has federal support: in 1878 the agent reported that Dull Knife's people "claimed that they did not enter into the agreement of September 26, 1876."
notes: The Little Wolf in the Arapaho list is in the statute too (an Arapaho of that name), so the layout is not garbled. ARCIA 1878 p. XXIII carries the Dull Knife denial.

source_title: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868
source_quote: hereby relinquish, release, and surrender to the United States all right, claim, and interest in and to all territory outside the two reservations above mentioned, except the right to roam and hunt
corrected_summary: Art. 2 did relinquish all territory outside the Medicine Lodge and Sioux reservations, keeping the right to roam and hunt. It also allowed attaching within a year to the Medicine Lodge agency, the planned Missouri River agency, or the Crow agency. Many Northern Cheyennes did live at Sioux agencies before 1877 (ARCIA 1878 says they were "taken from the Sioux country"), so "never located" is overstated. That non-fulfillment voids the cession is the author's legal argument, not a court holding.

source_title: Treaty with the Sioux, Apr. 29, 1868, Art. 2
source_quote: other friendly tribes or individual Indians as from time to time they may be willing, with the consent of the United States, to admit amongst them
corrected_summary: The 1868 Sioux treaty did provide for other friendly tribes to live on the Sioux reservation, but only if the Sioux were willing and the U.S. consented. So the U.S. could not place the Northern Cheyenne there on its own; it needed Sioux agreement. The author's statement that no such right existed at all is overstated.

source_title: Executive order of Nov. 26, 1884; Act of June 3, 1926
source_quote: set apart as a reserva tion for the use and occupation of the Northern Cheyenne Indians, now residing in the southern portion of Montana Territory
corrected_summary: The Northern Cheyenne had no reservation of their own from the 1868 treaty until the executive order of Nov. 26, 1884, about 16 years, not 20. Congress declared the reservation (as set by the 1900 order) tribal property only in 1926.
notes: "Exiled in their homeland" is the author's characterization.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024, Northern Cheyenne chapter
source_quote: Many people today have concluded that the Treaty of 1868 was made by a limited number of People
notes: Would be settled by the handwritten 1868 Fort Laramie council proceedings (NARA RG 75, Records of the Indian Peace Commission, 1867-68). The ratified text lists 14 Northern Cheyenne signers including Little Wolf and Dull Knife (15 Stat. 657-658).

source_title: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868
source_quote: the army to be present and attest the delivery of all the goods, herein named
corrected_summary: The treaty (Art. 6) did require an Army officer to attend and attest annuity deliveries. That it failed because of fraud is the author's view; the 1873 House frauds report was not checked.
notes: H.R. Rep. No. 98, 42d Cong., 3d sess. (1873) would settle the fraud point; not in the local library.

source_title: Act of Feb. 28, 1877, ch. 72, ratifying the agreement of Sept. 26, 1876; ARCIA 1878
source_quote: Nine hundred and thirty- seven of them arrived there on the 5th of August, 1877
corrected_summary: The Cheyenne marks on the 1876 agreement were made in September 1876, about ten months before the removal; 937 Northern Cheyennes reached the Cheyenne and Arapaho agency on Aug. 5, 1877. The commissioners could not have known in 1876 that the Cheyennes "had already been moved". The agreement itself (Art. 4) planned a removal to Indian Territory. It is fair to say the allotment and on-reservation terms became impossible for those removed in 1877.
notes: Endnotes 55-56 rest on the wrong 1877 signing date (see PSL-CHY-B-002).

source_title: ARCIA 1878 (Commissioner; Agent Miles); ARCIA 1879 (Agent Miles); Grinnell 1915

source_quote: As to suppliesof medicines, there was a scarcity, and many persons suffered and died for lack of proper remedies.
corrected_summary: After the 1877 surrender the Northern Cheyennes were taken to the Cheyenne and Arapaho agency at Darlington, near Fort Reno, not Fort Sill (937 arrived Aug. 5, 1877, per the Commissioner). Their agent admitted that medicines ordered in May 1878 did not arrive until Jan. 1879 and that "many persons suffered and died". Grinnell says nearly two-thirds of 999 fell sick within two months and 41 died that winter. "As many as one-third died" is Sandoz's estimate and is not supported by these sources.
notes: Agent Miles, Aug. 31, 1878 (ARCIA 1878 p. 56): about 2,000 sick on the reservation and deaths "which might have been obviated" with anti-malarial remedies. The source's repeated "Fort Sill" is an error.

corrected_summary: On Sept. 9, 1878 about 300 Northern Cheyennes (87 or 89 men by federal count) under Dull Knife and Little Wolf left the agency for the north. The federal reports also state that on the way through Kansas they killed more than forty settlers. The 350/92 figures, 13,000 troops and 1,000 miles are from the source's secondary authorities.
notes: The Kansas killings (Commissioner's figure) should appear alongside the exodus on the map; the Commissioner also blamed the Cheyennes' own conduct and denied ration shortfalls, while Agent Miles in 1879 admitted treaty rations "were not all furnished".

source_title: ARCIA 1879, Commissioner's report, "The remnant of Dull Knife's band"
source_quote: The prisoners numbered at this time forty-nine men, fifty-one women, and forty-eight children.
corrected_summary: Dull Knife's band was held prisoner at Camp Robinson after its Oct. 1878 capture. The Commissioner gives 148 prisoners (49 men, 51 women, 48 children), not 149 (46/61/42). The Indian Office itself had asked the War Department to send them to Fort Wallace, Kansas, for identification and prosecution, and on Jan. 3, 1879 the headmen were told they would be sent south.
notes: The quote "We have found the place we started to come to" was not checked (Grinnell/Powell).

notes: The Commissioner of Indian Affairs' own report confirms the food, fuel and water cutoff and Wild Hog being put in irons on Jan. 9. Grinnell 1915 (p. ~411) gives the same five days/three days and notes some Cheyennes said eight days. Wessells's testimony itself (Board of Officers, RG 98) was not reached.

corrected_summary: On the night of Jan. 9, 1879 the starving prisoners broke out; troops pursued and, by the Commissioner's own account, "most of their number were eventually killed". The same report says the prisoners had at least 15 guns and killed two sentinels. Grinnell records about fifty bodies brought in. The Army's 64 dead / 78 captured / 7 missing count, the Jan. 22 washout volleys and the civilian killings come from the Board of Officers proceedings, which were not reached.

corrected_summary: The reservation was created by executive order of Nov. 26, 1884 (the "16 November" date is wrong). Calling the order legally questionable is the author's argument; Congress declared the (1900) reservation tribal property in 1926 (44 Stat. 690).

source_quote: such offender shall forfeit and pay the sum of one thousand dollars. And it shall, moreover, be lawful for the President of the United States to take such measures, and to employ such military force
corrected_summary: The 1834 act imposed a $1,000 forfeiture on anyone settling on or surveying lands secured to a tribe by treaty, and made it lawful for the President to remove them by force. Removal was authorized, not required. The federal Peace Commission (1868) agreed the gold-rush miners had only a right of transit and took the land over Indian protests. source_quote: having had fully explained to us the amendment made on the 6th day of August, 1861, by the Senate of the United States
corrected_summary: The Senate struck Art. 11 (which asked that Denver-area proprietors be allowed to buy town lands at $1.25 an acre). The Statutes at Large print an assent to that amendment "in full council", dated [Oct. 29, 1861] and signed by the same ten chiefs, so "no evidence" of assent is wrong; whether that paper is genuine is the open question (see PSL-SCA-035). The 1864 act (13 Stat. 94) let the Arapahoe County probate judge enter the Denver town site at the minimum price; under U.S. law the land was by then ceded, so no tribal permission was sought. Reports that chiefs denied signing (Colley 1863) were not checked.
notes: The Seward letter (Aug. 12, 1861) asking that assent be obtained is consistent with the later paper assent. Keep the tribe's fraud allegation as an allegation.
